items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: Milt let me use one of his fiddles to make the gig.

ctx.x: But you've worked with everybody -- black, white.

Yes, I have worked with quite a few and I'm thankful that I have. I worked -- I'm going to tell you one gig with Bob Dorough (PHONETIC). He's a pianist, singer, the one that said (unintelligible) he said he did some things with Miles, which he did. Bob Dorough called me up and Al Schachtman, I believe it is -- he was the guitarist with Nina Simone when she first hit the scene. They had a bar mitzvah to play out in -- it wasn't, not Queens -- out in Long Island somewhere. Well, it was right around the corner from…
I'm the only brother there and so when Al and Bob

items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: teaching Milt Hinton Henry, he's out there teaching.

ctx.x: Well, more and more people are thinking about music education in terms of black music. It's like this tape. People are thinking about it in schools. But people that have had to learn the way you learned are going to have to come up with new approaches because the ones now are not adequate.
Well, that's true. Then there are some cats still out there-- teaching Milt Hinton Henry, he's out there teaching.
Max Mack has been teaching. There's Larry Ridley (PHONETIC), bass player, kid over in Jersey, has been teaching.
